title: LCIA Challenge Decision — Decision 9 (26/02/2019)
text:
DECISION RENDERED ON 26 FEBRUARY 2019
Subject: The First and Second Respondents challenged the entire Tribunal (entirely
selected by the LCIA Court) pursuant to Article 10 of the LCIA Rules 2014.
Outcome: Rejected
Seat: London, England
Governing Law of English law
the Contract:
Summary: The challenge related to procedural decisions and orders by the Tribunal,
including an Order that varied a buy-out mechanism as set out in the Tribunal’s
Second Award.
The LCIA Court rejected the challenge.
Given that the Parties opted for LCIA arbitration and chose London as the seat
of the arbitration, the law applicable to the challenge was English law, to be
considered together with the relevant provisions of the LCIA Rules.
The challenging Parties may not raise the issue of the validity, fairness or
appropriateness of an order issued by the Tribunal over four months earlier.
Pursuant to Article 10.3 of the LCIA Rules, they were required to file a
challenge within 14 days of becoming aware of the order.
Prior to making the Order at issue, the Tribunal heard submissions from both
sides and considered the fact that the mechanism for completion of the
transaction it had included in its Second Award did not appear to be working.
The Tribunal’s reasons in support of its Order were set out in some detail in
the Order. They are logical, coherent and based on relevant considerations.
There is no evidence to suggest that the Tribunal issued its Order for any
reason other than to seek to ensure that the Second Award would be
enforceable. The Tribunal may have been wrong as a matter of law as to
whether it could issue the Order, but there was nothing whatsoever to suggest
to the fair-minded and informed observer that the Tribunal did this because it
may have been biased against the relevant Parties.
As regards the Tribunal’s alleged failure to conduct the case with reasonable
efficiency, diligence and industry, it suffices for the LCIA Court to observe, as
regards diligence and industry, that having considered the expert opinions
filed in relation to the relevant issue, the Tribunal cannot be said to have been
clearly wrong in making the decision that it did; and as regards efficiency, that

the Tribunal cannot be criticised given the relatively short timeframe within
which it issued its order.
The Tribunal did not show bias where it conducted its own research on a
question it was called upon to decide, drew the attention of the Parties to an
authority the Tribunal considered may be relevant, and gave the Parties an
opportunity to comment upon it.
The Tribunal’s decision to suspend the proceedings pending resolution of the
challenge did not amount to a failure to act with reasonable efficiency,
diligence and industry. In the circumstances, it was not unreasonable for the
Tribunal to have considered that the arbitration ultimately would be better
served by the Parties and the Tribunal focusing on the challenge proceedings,
and for the case to resume and be completed after the challenge had been
determined.

Decision 9 - 4

I. OVERVIEW
1. This decision of a Division of the LCIA Court determines, in the name of the LCIA Court, an
Application by the First and Second Respondents under Article 10 of the LCIA Arbitration Rules 2014
(the LCIA Rules) against the three members of the Tribunal appointed by the LCIA Court to resolve a
dispute between the Parties (the Challenge).
2. The Division, after careful consideration of the facts, the law applicable to the Challenge and the
parties’ submissions, unanimously concludes that none of grounds raised in support of the Challenge
gives rise to justifiable doubts as to the Tribunal’s impartiality or independence, or establishes a failure
on the part of the Tribunal to act fairly or impartially as between the parties, or to conduct the
arbitration with reasonable efficiency, diligence and industry.
3. The Challenge is therefore dismissed. The costs of the Challenge are deferred, and are to be
determined and apportioned by the Tribunal as part of its decision under Article 28 of the LCIA Rules.
II. FACTUAL BACKGROUND
The Parties
4. The Claimant in the arbitration is […] a legal entity existing under the laws of the Principality of
Liechtenstein. The Claimant is represented in the Challenge proceedings by [Firm A].
5. The First and Second Respondents in the arbitration are […] two companies incorporated in the
British Virgin Islands. The First and Second Respondents are represented in the Challenge proceedings
by [Firm B]. The parties and the Tribunal have adopted the expression “[X] Shareholders” to refer to
the First and Second Respondents. For ease of reference, the Division adopts the same expression in
this decision.
Decision 9 - 5

6. The Third Respondent is [Y], a company incorporated in Malta. [Y] is the parent company of the [Y]
Group, which carries on business within [a certain region] through various subsidiaries operating in
the e-commerce sector. [Y] did not actively participate in the Challenge proceedings. A reference in
this decision to the “parties” refers collectively to the Claimant and the [X] Shareholders, whereas
“Parties” refers collectively to the Claimant and the three Respondents.
7. The Claimant has disclosed that its claim is being funded by a third-party funder, [Funder C], a
company that forms part of the [D] Group.
The Underlying Dispute
8. The [X] Shareholders’ application under Article 10 of the LCIA Rules was filed with enclosures
spanning some 350 pages. Voluminous additional correspondence, exhibits and expert reports
relating to the arbitration or the Challenge were subsequently provided to the Division. All of this
documentation was carefully reviewed by the Division. In this section of its decision, the Division offers
a non-exhaustive summary of the underlying dispute in order to provide context for the Challenge.
9. The Claimant and the [X] Shareholders are shareholders in [Y]. The Claimant holds [a certain] % of
the total issued shares in [Y], the First Respondent [a certain] %, and the Second Respondent [the
remaining] %.
10. The Claimant and the three Respondents are parties to a Shareholders’ Deed of Agreement
entered into on 11 August 2015 (the Shareholders’ Agreement). The Shareholders’ Agreement
contains an arbitration agreement providing for the settlement of disputes by binding arbitration
under the LCIA Rules, the seat and place of the arbitration to be London, England. The Shareholders’
Agreement also contains a governing law clause providing that the agreement and any dispute or
claim arising in connection with it or its subject matter shall be governed by English law.
Decision 9 - 6

11. The Claimant submitted its Request for Arbitration on 28 June 2016. The Claimant’s claims related
to the manner in which the affairs of [Y] and its subsidiaries were being conducted. It was alleged that
the conduct of the [X] Shareholders had been in their own self-interest and in disregard of the
Claimant’s rights. The Claimant submitted that the [X] Shareholders’ conduct was unfairly prejudicial,
oppressive and unfairly discriminatory.
12. The primary relief sought by the Claimant was an award providing that the Claimant’s shares in [Y]
shall be acquired by the [X] Shareholders and/or [Y] at a price to be determined by the Tribunal taking
into account the effects of the alleged unfairly prejudicial conduct.
13. The Respondents served Responses to the Request for Arbitration on 26 July 2016. The [X]
Shareholders denied the Claimant’s claims and averred that the purpose of the arbitration was to
attempt to extract from the [X] Shareholders more than the Claimant’s shares in [Y] are really worth.
The arbitration seems to have proceeded on the basis that there had been an irretrievable breakdown
in the relationship between the Claimant and the [X] Shareholders.
14. By decision dated 3 August 2016, the LCIA Court appointed [Arbitrator E], [Arbitrator F] and
[Arbitrator G] as members of the Tribunal, without nomination by the Parties, with [Arbitrator G]
presiding.
15. Between 25 September and 5 October 2017, the Tribunal presided over a nine-day merits hearing.
In the course of the hearing, the Tribunal made an order bifurcating the proceedings between liability
and quantum.
16. On 21 March 2018, the Tribunal rendered a Partial Final Award on liability (the First Award). The
Tribunal found in favour of the Claimant and ordered the [X] Shareholders to acquire the Claimant’s
shares in [Y]. The price to be paid for the Claimant’s shares would be determined by the Tribunal in
Decision 9 - 7

the subsequent quantum phase of the arbitration, on the basis of various decisions and assumptions
set out in the First Award.
17. On 18 April 2018, the [X] Shareholders applied to the English High Court under Section 68 of the
Arbitration Act 1996 (the Act) to set aside the First Award. The [X] Shareholders alleged serious
irregularity affecting the Tribunal, the proceedings and the award, on grounds that it is useful to cite
at this juncture.
…the Tribunal (i) failed to comply with its general duties under Section 33 of the Arbitration Act 1996
to act fairly and impartially as between the parties, because the Tribunal’s Chairman breached his duty
of impartiality and independence and was biased; (ii) failed to conduct the arbitration in accordance
with the procedure agreed by the parties, because the Tribunal referred to documents that had not
been admitted into the evidential records in accordance with the procedure that had been agreed
between the Tribunal and the parties; and (iii) failed to deal with the issues that were put to it, because
it failed to address a number of the Claimants’ arguments.
18. The apparent bias complained of in paragraph (i), above, was said to arise from alleged personal
and professional relationships between, on the one hand, the presiding arbitrator and, on the other,
the Claimant’s senior counsel, one of the Claimant’s solicitors, as well as a representative of the
Claimant’s funder (see the [X] Shareholders’ correspondence of 2 January 2019, para. 1.5).
19. Following a valuation hearing that took place on 10-11 April 2018, the Tribunal issued a second
Partial Final Award on 16 July 2018 (the Second Award), fixing at US$ 67,159,546 the price to be paid
by the [X] Shareholders for the Claimant’s shares.
20. The Tribunal included in the dispositive section of the Second Award a mechanism setting out the
steps by which the parties, within 28 days of the Second Award (i.e. by 13 August 2018), were to
implement and close the sale and purchase of the Claimant’s shares, an operation referred to in the
Dispositif as the “Transaction”. The last paragraph of the Dispositif reads as follows (para. 200(v)):
Decision 9 - 8

(v) Save that the Tribunal remains seised of any issues arising in respect of the implementation
and completion of the Transaction and/or in respect of interest and costs, all and any other
claims and counterclaims are hereby dismissed.
21. On 8 August 2018, the [X] Shareholders issued an application under Section 68 of the Act
challenging the Second Award. The application was based on the first of the grounds listed in the
previous Section 68 application, namely apparent bias on the part of the presiding arbitrator.
22. Early in August 2018, the [X] Shareholders brought to the attention of the Tribunal two recent
developments that were said to stand as obstacles to the Claimant being in a position to deliver, before
the deadline set out in the Second Award, the share certificate(s) in relation to its shareholdings in [Y]
“free of restrictions”. The first was the position adopted by [a foreign Regulator) that prior consent of
the [Regulator] was required before the Claimant’s shares could be transferred to the [X]
Shareholders; the second that a petition to wind up [Y] had been presented to the Maltese courts by
[Petitioner H].
23. On 6 August 2018, the Claimant applied to the Tribunal to request modifications to the mechanism
set out in the Second Award for the completion of the Transaction, relying on the Tribunal’s reserved
jurisdiction under paragraph 200(v) of the Second Award. The reason for the application was that, in
order for the mechanism to be respected, Claimant’s counsel would have to comply with UK anti-
money laundering legislation, which required obtaining information about the [X] Shareholders and
their beneficial owners. The [X] Shareholders objected to the Claimant’s application on the basis that
the Second Award was incapable of amendment in the manner proposed by the Claimant.
24. By an order dated 19 August 2018 (the 19 August Order), the Tribunal granted the Claimant’s
application and varied the buy-out mechanism set out in the Second Award.
Decision 9 - 9

25. On 28 August 2018, the Claimant applied for the 19 August Order to be converted into an award.
The [X] Shareholders objected to this application and the Tribunal ultimately rejected it as part of an
order dated 18 October 2018.
26. On 10 September 2018, the [X] Shareholders issued Notices of Discontinuance of their Section 68
applications. According to the [X] Shareholders, the reason for the discontinuances was that the First
and Second Awards had become unenforceable because the buy-out mechanism had failed by reason
of the Claimant’s failure to deliver its share certificate(s). The [X] Shareholders took the position that
since the Tribunal was functus officio, no other buy-out mechanism could be substituted.
27. The costs for the discontinued Section 68 applications then became an issue between the Claimant
and the [X] Shareholders, seemingly against the backdrop of the Claimant giving consideration to an
application to set aside the Notices of Discontinuance so as not to find itself exposed in other
proceedings to the contentions set out in the Section 68 applications […]. In the event, the parties
entered into a consent order (the 9 October Consent Order) by which the [X] Shareholders “undertook
that they would not rely on any facts and matters which are the same or substantially the same as
those relating to the Section 68 claims in any proceedings in any jurisdiction." (para. 14)
28. On 26 September 2018, the [X] Shareholders applied to the Tribunal for an order that the Claimant
make available for inspection the original of any share certificate(s) in respect of its holdings in [Y]. As
part of its order of 18 October 2018, the Tribunal ordered that the Claimant allow inspection of the
original share certificate(s). The inspection took place the following day. Shortly thereafter, the [X]
Shareholders raised various concerns about the Claimant’s share certificate, which came to be
referred to as the re-issued share certificate, or “RISC”. In an email dated 26 October 2018, the [X]
Shareholders asked the Claimant to answer a number of questions about the RISC.
Decision 9 - 10

29. On 6 November 2018, the [X] Shareholders applied to the Tribunal for an order that [Y] produce
documents relating to the reissuance of the RISC to the Claimant. By order dated 23 November 2018,
the Tribunal ordered the Claimant and [Y] to produce the Claimant’s request for a replacement
certificate and a certified copy of [Y’s] share register. The Tribunal also asked the [X] Shareholders, in
the event they intended to maintain their allegation that the RISC was a forgery, to set out in writing
the precise grounds supporting that allegation and the evidence upon which they relied.
30. The [X] Shareholders responded to this request in a letter dated 30 November 2018. That same
letter requested, on the basis of the seriousness of the issue and its relevance to the question of costs,
that there be a full hearing to enable the Tribunal to consider the authenticity of the RISC and the
circumstances of its issuance by [Y].
31. A one-day hearing had been scheduled on 14 January 2019 for the Tribunal to hear submissions
on the question of costs and interest, with 15 January being held in reserve.
32. On 12 December 2018, the [X] Shareholders reiterated their request for a full hearing to consider
the issues raised in respect of the RISC and asked the Tribunal to direct the Claimant to provide a
detailed response to the questions in their email of 26 October 2018 and to serve witness statements
from the relevant individuals at the Claimant, [Funder C], [Y] and [Firm A] who were involved in the
reissuance of the RISC, together with disclosure of all documents relevant to the reissuance. The [X]
Shareholders also suggested that the 14 January 2019 hearing be postponed to enable the parties
adequately to prepare and present their cases.
33. On 19 December 2018, the Tribunal issued an order (the 19 December Order) denying the further
disclosure and production of witness statements in relation to the RISC that had been requested by
the [X] Shareholders. The Tribunal also denied the request for a postponement of the 14 January 2019
Decision 9 - 11

hearing. In this same order, the Tribunal indicated that it would entertain at the hearing oral argument
and submissions on the question of the validity of the RISC, in light of the [X] Shareholders’ submission
(objected to by the Claimant) that this question was relevant to the determination of costs by the
Tribunal.
34. On 30 December 2018, at 7:04 PM, GMT, the [X] Shareholders wrote to the Tribunal to request
that the Tribunal recall its 19 August Order (the Recall Application). The [X] Shareholders gave the
Tribunal until noon, GMT, on 2 January 2019 to do so. The [X] Shareholders concluded the Recall
Application with an express reservation of their right to make an application under Article 10 of the
LCIA Rules.
35. On 1 January 2019, the Administrative Secretary to the Tribunal informed the parties of the
Tribunal’s decision to decline to comply with the [X] Shareholders’ request within the stipulated
deadline. The relevant extract of the Tribunal’s decision reads as follows:
The [X] Shareholders imposed a deadline of noon on Wednesday 2 January 2019 within which they
require the Tribunal to recall the 19 August Order. The Tribunal declines to comply for three reasons:
first, the members of the Tribunal are not in a position to deliberate as they would wish to do until all
of its members return to their offices after the Christmas/New Year break. Second, such a step in
respect of an Order made over four months ago could not be taken before Claimant had been afforded
a proper opportunity to comment upon this application. Third, the [X] Shareholders sought (and were
granted) a postponement of the 2 January 2019 deadline for their reply to Claimant’s 27 December
2018 application until 5 p.m. GMT, on 7 January 2019 in order to accommodate their and their
advisors’ unavailability over the holiday period. It would be unreasonable if they were to deny
Claimant (and the members of the Tribunal) a similar indulgence. emphasis in the original
36. On 2 January 2019, shortly after the filing of their Article 10 Application, the [X] Shareholders
proposed that in order to avoid wasted costs, the 14 January 2019 hearing be postponed until the LCIA
Court has ruled on the Challenge. This was objected to by the Claimant and the Tribunal decided, on
the same day, that the hearing fixed for 14 (and 15) January 2019 would proceed.
Decision 9 - 12

37. At the 14 January 2019 hearing, the Tribunal heard submissions on costs and interest, as well as
the issues raised by the [X] Shareholders concerning the RISC. The parties also discussed the [X]
Shareholders’ Recall Application. In connection with the latter, on 18 January 2019 the Tribunal issued
a memorandum (the 18 January Memorandum) inviting the parties, if they so wished, to comment
on certain authorities cited in the memorandum on the issue of whether the Tribunal had jurisdiction
to modify the Second Award by its 19 August Order. The deadline set for the filing of these comments
was 25 January 2019.
38. On 25 January 2019, the [X] Shareholders filed detailed comments on the authorities cited in the
18 January Memorandum and submitted an expert report of [Expert I] in support of their position.
The Claimant responded to this submission by letter dated 5 February 2019, to which were attached
two expert reports: an expert report of [Expert J] dated 5 February 2019, and an expert report of
[Expert K] dated 20 December 2018. [Expert K]’s report had been prepared for filing before the courts
of BVI. While its focus is on the enforceability of the Second Award, [Expert K] also comments on the
question of whether the Tribunal had jurisdiction to vary its Second Award by making the 19 August
Order. [Expert J] refers to [Expert K]’s view on this question in his report. On 8 February 2019, the [X]
Shareholders – arguing that procedural fairness dictates they should be given a right to reply to the
Claimant’s 5 February 2019 submission – replied to the Claimant’s response and filed a rebuttal expert
report by [Expert I].
39. Meanwhile, on 22 January 2019, the [X] Shareholders had applied to the Tribunal for an order
compelling the Claimant to withdraw an application before the courts of Cyprus against a number of
Defendants, including the [X] Shareholders. The [X] Shareholders submitted that these proceedings
had been instituted in breach of Article 25.3 of the LCIA Rules.
Decision 9 - 13

40. On 28 January 2019, the Tribunal granted this application in part, and issued a direction that the
Claimant not pursue such part of its application to the Cyprus courts that relates to the issues of costs
and interest that are still pending before the Tribunal, unless and until an application to the Tribunal
has been duly made pursuant to Article 25.3 of the LCIA Rules.
41. On 1 February 2019, in response to the [X] Shareholders’ letter of 30 January 2019 – issued in
connection with the Challenge and which is summarised below – the Tribunal decided to suspend the
arbitration until such time as the Division has had an opportunity to determine the Challenge. The
Tribunal maintained this decision on 4 February 2019, and again on 6 February 2019.
42. On 5 February 2019, the [X] Shareholders applied to the Tribunal for a peremptory order requiring
the Claimant to comply with the Tribunal’s direction of 28 January 2019, with a view, in the event of
non-compliance, to applying to the High Court for an order requiring the Claimant to comply. In light
of the Tribunal’s decision to suspend the arbitration pending determination of the Challenge, the
Claimant indicated in an email dated 6 February 2019 that it would not respond to this application
until further direction from the Tribunal. On 8 February 2019, the Tribunal put the Claimant on notice
that, in the event the arbitration resumes under the presently constituted Tribunal, the Claimant
would be required to submit its comments on the application with 24 hours of the resumption.
The Challenge – Procedural History
43. As already mentioned, the [X] Shareholders filed their application to the LCIA Court under Article
10 of the LCIA Rules on 2 January 2019.
44. Upon receipt of the Challenge, the Claimant informed the Tribunal and the LCIA that it intended
to object to the Challenge. Later in the day on 2 January 2019, the Administrative Secretary to the
Tribunal informed the parties and the LCIA that the Tribunal would respond to the matters raised in
Decision 9 - 14

the Challenge in due course and to the extent that it deemed it appropriate. The Tribunal added that
in the absence of agreement between the Parties to an adjournment of the 14(15) January 2019
hearing, the arbitration should not be suspended and the scheduled hearing would proceed.
45. On 3 January 2019, the LCIA acknowledged receipt of the Challenge, the Claimant’s email objecting
to the Challenge and the Tribunal’s above-mentioned email. The LCIA indicated that in accordance
with Article 10.6 of the LCIA Rules, unless the parties so agreed or the Tribunal resigned by 16 January
2019, the LCIA Court would decide the Challenge. The LCIA Court granted the Claimant, the Third
Respondent and the Tribunal until 11 January 2019 to comment on the Challenge.
46. By email dated 3 January 2019, the Tribunal requested (and was subsequently granted) an
extension until 25 January 2019 to comment on the Challenge. In the same email, members of the
Tribunal indicated that they rejected all of the allegations raised in support of the Challenge, and
stated that they would not resign. The Tribunal also referred to the text of its email to the parties
dated 1 January 2019 to refute the allegation in the Challenge that the Tribunal had “refused” to recall
its 19 August Order as requested by the [X] Shareholders in their email of 30 December 2018. The
Tribunal emphasised that what was decided on 1 January 2019 was simply to decline the invitation to
recall this order by noon, GMT, on 2 January 2019, a deadline so near as to make it unfeasible for the
Claimant to comment on the [X] Shareholders’ request.
47. On 15 January 2019, the [X] Shareholders wrote to correct their application insofar as it alleged
that the Tribunal had refused to recall its 19 August Order, Counsel explaining that they had
misconstrued the wording of the Tribunal’s email of 1 January 2019.
48. On 17 January 2019, the Tribunal filed with the LCIA the “Tribunal’s Response to the [X]
Shareholders’ Article 10 Application dated 2 January 2019”.
Decision 9 - 15

49. On 24 January 2019, the Claimant submitted comments on the Challenge.
50. On 29 January 2019, the LCIA notified the Parties that, pursuant to Article 10.6 of the LCIA Rules
and Article D.3(c) of the Constitution of the LCIA Court, the LCIA Court had appointed [L], [M] and [N],
to be the Division in this arbitration to determine the Challenge, with [N] acting as chair of the Division.
51. On 30 January 2019, the [X] Shareholders wrote to the LCIA Court in reply to the Tribunal’s
Response dated 17 January 2019, and to update the LCIA and the Division on recent developments in
the arbitration that were relevant to the Challenge.
52. On 1 February 2019, the Tribunal submitted five points in reply to the [X] Shareholders’ letter of
30 January 2019. Attached to the Tribunal’s email was a copy of the skeleton argument on forgery
dated 9 January 2019 filed by the [X] Shareholders in connection with the 14 January 2019 hearing, as
well as the judgment […] dated 30 January 2019 in the High Court proceedings between the [X]
Shareholders, the Claimant and [Y]. The Tribunal drew the Division’s attention to paragraph 14 of the
judgment, where reference is made to the [X] Shareholders’ undertaking in the 9 October Consent
Order, already referred to in this decision at paragraph 27 above. As already mentioned, it is in this
email communication of 1 February 2019 that the Tribunal advised the Parties and the LCIA Court of
its decision to suspend the arbitration pending the determination of the Challenge.
53. On 4 February 2019, the Division issued its first communication to the Parties to inform them of
the procedure that the Division proposed to follow to determine the Challenge. Having regard to the
[X] Shareholders’ request that the Challenge be determined “as a matter of urgency” and the
Tribunal’s decision to suspend the proceedings pending the determination of the Challenge, the
Division proposed a short briefing schedule affording the Parties and the Tribunal an opportunity to
complete the submissions already made and the documents already filed in relation to the Challenge.
Decision 9 - 16

54. The proposed briefing schedule contemplated the Claimant filing supplemental comments on the
Challenge by Friday 8 February 2019, the [X] Shareholders filing their final submissions by Wednesday
13 February 2019, and the Tribunal providing additional comments (if any) on the Challenge by
Monday 18 February 2019. The Division invited confirmation from the Parties and the Tribunal that
the procedure and deadlines proposed by the Division were acceptable to them.
55. On 5 February 2019, the Tribunal wrote to the Division to confirm that it would provide its
additional comments on the Challenge by Monday 18 February 2019. In light of the representations
on the part of the [X] Shareholders contained in their correspondence of 4 February 2019, the Tribunal
reiterated that “the current suspension of the Arbitration is subject to any directions that the Division
or the LCIA Court might give.”
56. Later on 5 February 2019, the Tribunal wrote to the Division to bring to its attention a letter of
even date by which the [X] Shareholders had applied to the Tribunal for a peremptory order requiring
the Claimant to comply with the Tribunal’s direction of 28 January 2019 relating to the Cyprus
proceedings. The Tribunal sought the Division’s guidance in respect of the [X] Shareholders’ latest
application as a matter of urgency.
57. On 5 February 2019, the Claimant, among others, responded to the Division’s letter to the Parties
of 4 February 2019 and the recent correspondence exchange with the Tribunal. The Claimant noted
that the Claimant and the Respondents were in agreement that the arbitration proceedings were at a
critical stage and that any suspension of the proceedings should be avoided. The Claimant added, in
response to the Division’s letter of 4 February 2019, that it had no further comment to make on the
Challenge. In light of the urgency of the proceedings, the Claimant suggested that the remainder of
the Division’s proposed timetable be brought forward accordingly.
Decision 9 - 17

58. Later on 5 February 2019, the Division wrote in response to the correspondence received earlier
in the day from the Tribunal and the parties. The Division noted that it was conscious of the difficulty
– for the Parties and the Tribunal – resulting from the concurrent pendency of the Challenge and of
application(s) to the Tribunal in relation to matters considered urgent by one or more of the Parties
to the arbitration. The Division added that it intended to deal with the Challenge expeditiously, all the
while ensuring, consistent with the LCIA Rules, that the parties have a reasonable opportunity to be
heard in relation to the Challenge and that the challenged arbitrators are able to exercise their right
to comment on the Challenge. The Division indicated that it was agreeable to bringing forward the
briefing schedule it had initially proposed, such that any submissions in relation to the Challenge by
the [X] Shareholders would be due by Friday 8 February 2019, and any additional comments on the
Challenge by the Tribunal would be filed by Wednesday 13 February 2019. In response to the
Tribunal’s request for guidance from the Division in respect of the [X] Shareholders’ application for a
peremptory order, the Division indicated that beyond confirming its willingness and availability to deal
with the Challenge expeditiously, it considered that it was ultimately for the Tribunal to determine, in
light of recent developments, including the parties’ stated preference that the arbitration not be
suspended, whether it wished to revisit, or maintain, its decision to suspend the arbitration
proceedings pending the determination of the Challenge.
59. On 6 February 2019, the [X] Shareholders confirmed that they would be filing further submissions
in connection with the Challenge. In the interest of having the Challenge determined expeditiously,
the [X] Shareholders agreed to file these further submissions by Friday 8 February 2019.
60. Also on 6 February 2019, the Tribunal wrote to express confidence that it would be able to submit
its final comments on the Challenge on or before 13 February 2019, provided no new points of
Decision 9 - 18

substance were raised by the [X] Shareholders in their submission to be filed on 8 February 2019. The
Tribunal also confirmed that it was maintaining the suspension of the proceedings.
61. As agreed, the [X] Shareholders’ final submissions were filed on 8 February 2019. The Tribunal’s
additional comments on the Challenge were filed on 11 February 2019. On that same date, the
Division acknowledged receipt of these submissions and indicated that it considered the Challenge
proceedings to be closed.

within 14 days prior to the date the challenge was issued;

2. The Tribunal’s Decision to Suspend the Arbitration

of the Tribunal’s powers and was taken contrary to the Tribunal’s duty, under Article 14.4(ii) of the

suspension, and therefore do not appear to be arguing that the suspension evidences unfair treatment

a challenge is being considered. While the Tribunal may consider it appropriate to suspend the
proceedings pending the determination of a challenge, in the experience of the Division suspension
of the arbitration is not the usual course to take.

Tribunal was right or wrong to suspend the proceedings, a decision which falls within its discretion.
